abstract_summary: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in comp...

as follows:
Learned memory control for SAM-based trackers.We formulate memory bank control in SAM-
based trackers as an MDP over a fixed-capacity bank. The state describes the content of the bank, the
action selects the entry to evict, and the reward scores the resulting prediction against the annotation.
This formulation allows the memory control to be learned instead of being manually designed.
State-of-the-art visual object tracker.We present SAM3RL, which extends SAM 3 with a mem-
ory controller obtained by optimizing the introduced MDP with RL. It improves over SAM 3 on 11
out of 12 benchmarks and ranks first on 10 of them. The largest gains are achieved on the VOT(S)
challenges, with+3.6on VOTS 2026 and+5.5on VOT-LT 2022. It is also the only tracker that con-
sistently succeeds in video object segmentation, scoring+1.1on MOSE v2 and+2.5on SA-V val.
2

SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
Training data.We train on the LaSOT training split (Fan et al., 2019), whose 1,120 sequences are
divided into 896 for training and 224 for validation, while the official test set is held out. LaSOT is
annotated with per-frame bounding boxes at 30 FPS. Since consecutive frames at that rate are nearly
identical, an eviction decision changes the bank very little while still consuming a decision step. We
therefore subsample every sixth frame, so that training episodes run at 5 FPS and span 425 decision
steps on average. This also matches the typical annotation rate of VOS datasets.

from this bootstrap, we keep the critic out of the targets and use it only as a baseline, as it fits the
training videos well but transfers poorly to unseen videos. Each of the 400 iterations collects 376-
step rollouts from 256 parallel environments. Training takes about 24 hours on four H200 GPUs.
We evaluate the greedy policy on the full validation videos every 25 iterations and select the best
checkpoint. All remaining hyperparameters are listed in Table 13 in Appendix D.
Inference.The actor picks actions greedily, and its only overhead is a single MLP evaluation per
memory update. To keep the decision rate close to the 5 FPS seen in training, the memory controller
operates with a strides=round(ν/5), whereνis the frame rate of the benchmark.

average gain drops from 2.9 to
1.8 points. We therefore match the training rate with the strides, which requires the frame rate
to be known in advance and keeps the skipped frames out of the memory bank. The former is
rarely restrictive in practice, as the frame rate is usually available. Training at the native rate would
remove this restriction, but most decisions would then concern near-identical frames. Such a policy
could nonetheless exploit the skipped frames and improve further on high-frame-rate benchmarks.
Second, the policy controls only the seven frames in the memory bank, while the nine object pointers
are filled by a fixed rule. Learning both jointly is a natural direction for future work.

The states t groups the per-slot features into four disjoint groups: temporal, confidence, semantic,
and geometry; see Section 3.1. We test whether each group is necessary or sufficient with delete-one
and keep-one ablations, respectively. The former removes one group from the actor input, while the
latter keeps exactly one. Everything else, including the critic input, is unchanged. The groups differ
in the input size, with the baseline actor input having 1,560 dimensions after the pointer projection,
of which semantic take 1,152, temporal 256, geometry 120, and confidence 32. The performance is
presented in Tables 14 and 15 as a mean over three seeds for each arm. No single group is critically
necessary, and no single group is sufficient either. All arms still improve over SAM 3, except the
keep-one arms on MOSEv2, yet none matches the all-inputs actor across all benchmarks.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline outcomes are measured on held-out external benchmarks and official challenge servers using standard metrics, independent of the PPO reward signal used for training.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard benchmark metrics (Quality F-score, AUC, J&F) on held-out VOTS, VOT-LT, LaSOT, DiDi, and VOS datasets, including official evaluation servers.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: PPO training on LaSOT with reward equal to IoU tracking quality normalized by the SAM 3 default-memory baseline.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims of outperforming hand-crafted heuristics and achieving state-of-the-art results across most benchmarks without inference runtime penalty are directly corroborated by standard benchmark tables, official evaluation server submissions, and throughput measurements.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation spans 12-15 diverse tracking and VOS benchmarks (including VOTS challenges, VOT-LT, LaSOT, and MOSEv2), comparing against multiple hand-crafted heuristics ported to SAM 3 as well as native SAM 2 baselines, accompanied by multi-seed ablations.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluation is conducted on independent standard external tracking and segmentation test sets scored via standard toolkits and remote servers, showing consistent improvements over baselines.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard benchmark evaluation metrics (Quality F-score, AUC, J&F) scored across held-out external benchmark sets and official challenge evaluation servers (e.g., VOTS, VOT-LT, MOSEv2, SA-V).
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: PPO reinforcement learning on IoU tracking quality normalized by baseline default SAM 3 tracking performance on the LaSOT training split.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly discuss limitations regarding fixed stride matching pre-known frame rates, the lack of full joint learning for auxiliary object pointers, and qualitative failure cases during rapid viewpoint/scale changes.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, describing the 7-slot eviction action space, the 4-part state representation, reward normalization against a default baseline, PPO training setup on LaSOT, and strided inference matching the 5 FPS training frequency.
primary.quality_rationale: This is a rigorous, high-quality empirical study that identifies and fixes undocumented issues in foundation tracking models, systematically evaluates across standard benchmarks, and validates design choices via complete ablations.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper presents SAM3RL (and SAM2RL), formulating memory bank control for SAM-based visual object trackers as an MDP optimized with PPO on training sequences, eliminating hand-crafted eviction heuristics.

scholarly_quality.rationale: This is a rigorous, high-quality empirical study that identifies and fixes undocumented issues in foundation tracking models, systematically evaluates across standard benchmarks, and validates design choices via complete ablations.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly discuss limitations regarding fixed stride matching pre-known frame rates, the lack of full joint learning for auxiliary object pointers, and qualitative failure cases during rapid viewpoint/scale changes.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.
